A fridge keeps its eggs at much the same warmth from day to day, so that I know where a fridge egg begins. Boiling water: lower the eggs into water already at a full boil, and the clock begins as they go in; they peel more easily. Keep it boiling: the fire holds the water at a full boil till the eggs come out, and the quantity of water is of little moment. Fire out, lid on: the eggs once in boiling water, put out the fire and put on the lid, and the hot water finishes the eggs as it cools. This spares fewel; but the water does all the labour, so that its quantity decides the time, and too little cannot finish the work. If you choose this, measure it.

When the eggs come out, the heat in the white continues its progress inward, and the yolk cooks on for some minutes. Iced water carries the heat away fastest, and therefore arrests it soonest, and permits me to offer the softest yolks; a cold tap is nearly as good. Still air takes away scarcely any heat: to a hot egg upon the table it is less a means of cooling than a lid. For this I make allowance; but it forbids the softest yolks, and how much more the yolk will cook is not easily foretold.

The quantity of water in the pan, the eggs not reckoned. It signifies most with the fire out, when the water's own heat does the cooking: more water holds its heat longer. It signifies a little with the fire lit, because cold eggs entering boiling water cool a little water more than a great deal. And I remember how long each quantity you use takes to boil; it is therefore worth measuring.

How many eggs go in together. Cold eggs take heat from boiling water as they enter, and more eggs take more; so the water is longer in recovering, or, with the fire out, never recovers. For eggs begun in cold water it makes no difference to my computation: you tap when the water boils, and that already reckons them.

The higher you are, the less the air presses down, and the cooler water boils; and cooler water cooks more slowly. The difference accumulates: a kitchen upon a mountain needs sensibly longer than one by the sea. Tell me nearly how high you are, and I shall cook at the boiling point here shewn.

The cooling is likewise to be counted. An egg taken from the water continues some minutes to cook from within; iced water stops it soonest, and the table scarcely retards it. To leave the fire is not to leave the heat.

Upon the table, still air draws off heat so slowly, that the yolk ends within a fraction of a degree of where it would, had the egg never cooled at all. [README §5](https://github.com/danmackinlay/actual_egg_timer#5-carryover-the-cooling-step-is-part-of-the-recipe).

How to make this more reliable
Use eggs straight from the fridge. I know how cold a fridge is; a room can be a few degrees either way, and that moves the time.
Weigh the egg instead of picking a size. One size on the box covers eggs that need quite different times.
Put the eggs straight into ice water when they come out. On the counter the yolk keeps cooking, by an amount that is hard to predict.
Use more water. With the heat off, more water holds its heat for longer, so small differences in how fast it cools matter less.
I haven't learned anything yet. I learn how fast your stove boils water when you tap the boil, and your eggs when you tell me how one came out.
